name: Drafting Statements and Disclosures
title: Drafting Statements and Disclosures
answer: Drafting statements and disclosures covers the preparation of financial statements, the notes that accompany them, and the narrative sections of regulatory filings. It includes the primary statements, accounting policy notes, significant estimates, and management commentary. The work sits between the ledger close and the final filing, where numbers and words must agree. It also covers disclosure checklists and the mapping of line items to required taxonomies. This scope does not extend to the underlying accounting judgments, which remain with qualified professionals.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Drafting statements and disclosures covers the preparation of financial statements, the notes that accompany them, and the narrative sections of regulatory filings. It includes the primary statements, accounting policy notes, significant estimates, and management commentary. The work sits between the ledger close and the final filing, where numbers and words must agree. It also covers disclosure checklists and the mapping of line items to required taxonomies. This scope does not extend to the underlying accounting judgments, which remain with qualified professionals.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the general ledger and consolidation systems that hold the reported numbers, together with disclosure management software and document templates. Data flows from ERP and subledger systems into a reporting warehouse, where account mappings and validation rules are applied. Large language models and retrieval systems can draft narrative text by drawing on accounting standards, prior filings, and internal policy documents. Version control, access controls, and audit trails sit underneath, because every change to a disclosure must be traceable. Spreadsheets still appear at the edges, often for last mile adjustments and tie outs.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The typical process starts with a trial balance and supporting schedules, which are mapped to line items and disclosure requirements. A model or rules engine then produces a first draft of the notes and narrative, using templates and prior period language as a starting point. Controllers and technical accountants review the draft, check completeness against a disclosure checklist, and tie every figure back to the source. Consistency checks compare the statements, the notes, and the management commentary for contradictions or stale wording. The final version is locked, signed off, and passed to auditors or regulators with a record of who changed what.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on confidentiality, provenance, and review. Non public financial data must stay within approved systems, and any model used to draft text needs clear boundaries on what it can access and retain. Provenance means keeping a record of the source data, the model version, the prompts, and the human edits that produced the final disclosure. Firms typically require a named reviewer to sign off on AI assisted text, because the responsibility for the filing does not transfer to the tool. Risks include hallucinated disclosures, inconsistent wording across documents, and the accidental release of material information. Internal control over financial reporting and audit trail requirements shape how these tools are deployed.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more structured and continuous disclosure, with inline XBRL and digital tagging becoming standard in many jurisdictions. AI drafting tools are likely to move from first draft generation to ongoing consistency monitoring across quarterly and annual filings. Regulators and auditors are paying closer attention to how AI generated text is reviewed and evidenced, so traceability will matter more than raw speed. Integration with audit workflows and with the close process will continue, reducing the handoffs between spreadsheets and disclosure systems. The human reviewer remains central, because judgment about materiality and recognition cannot be delegated to a drafting tool.
